description:
I am looking for people who are curious, eager to learn, and interested in being part of a different kind of experience. I would like to build a team with members who enjoy sharing ideas and expressing their opinions, discussing different points of view, and finding ways to combine their knowledge and skills to grow and create something together.

You don't need to be an expert in any particular subject. The most important things are initiative, commitment, and a willingness to learn new things.
summary: ASTRA: The Last Hope is an educational space simulation video game that teaches mission engineering through hands-on learning. We developed a playable HTML demo featuring a cinematic intro, an Earth-to-Moon tutorial, and five missions of increasing difficulty (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune). Players configure their spacecraft (structure, power, communications, and science payload), choose a launch vehicle and orbit, and balance six resources: mass, power, budget, data, communications, and time. During the journey, they dodge asteroids and, if damage occurs, perform a scientifically explained extravehicular repair through a minigame. The game can be played solo or in teams of up to four people.
details:
Project Details

What does it do and how does it work?
ASTRA is a space simulator where the player experiences the lifecycle of a NASA mission: defining objectives, designing the spacecraft, verifying systems, and executing the mission. The player first configures the structure, power, communications, and science payload, and selects a launch vehicle and orbit. Then they travel through the solar system (an Earth-to-Moon tutorial and five missions: Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune), monitoring mass, power, budget, data, communications, and time. Along the way, they dodge asteroids; if the ship is damaged, a three-step cycle begins: diagnosis, an extravehicular repair minigame, and an expert report. It can be played solo or in teams of up to four people.

Benefits
It turns abstract concepts (payload, power consumption, communication delay, radiation) into decisions with visible consequences. It requires no prior knowledge or installation: it runs in the browser.

Expected impact
To spark curiosity about astronomy and aerospace engineering in students, and to introduce them to real mission design practices. It can be used in the classroom for collaborative work.

Tools used

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with no external libraries.
  • Graphics with <canvas> and sound with the Web Audio API.
  • localStorage to save progress.
  • Press Start 2P and VT323 fonts (Google Fonts).
  • Visual Studio Code as the code editor.
  • Power Point
  • Microsoft Clipchamp

Creativity
It combines technical rigor with storytelling: a survival-themed cinematic, reports in which the character explains the science behind each repair, and a secret suspense ending (“Anomaly detected… To be continued”). The retro aesthetic makes it appealing to young people.

Factors considered

  • Scientific accuracy: NASA data, real missions such as MOXIE and BioNutrients-2, and the methodology from Levri (2025).
  • Feasibility: lateral obstacle dodging instead of complex orbital simulations.
  • Progression: increasing difficulty, with a smaller resource margin on each planet.
  • Pedagogy: learning by doing, with brief explanations and no excess theory.
  • Accessibility: runs on any device with a browser.
  • Teamwork: roles and joint decision-making.
